bible.visualPremise: A flat 2D stickman-doodle explainer that traces one persistent misconception about Viking helmets across time: archaeological finds, Bronze Age ritual objects, 19th-century theater and Romantic art, and modern mass culture.
bible.visualTone: clear-eyed and slightly wry — authoritative but approachable, with moments of dramatic showmanship when illustrating the myth and sober, documentary calm when showing the archaeological record.

styleContract.illustrationStyle: Simplified stickman/doodle explainer construction — circle heads, dot eyes, stick limbs, mitten hands — never a detailed or semi-realistic character
styleContract.lineLanguage: Uniform thin, clean black outlines of identical weight everywhere; no sketchiness, no variable line weight, no cross-hatching
styleContract.shapeLanguage: Simple geometric primitives — circles, rounded rectangles, straight or gently curved lines — never intricate or organic detail
styleContract.detailLevel: Minimal — enough to read instantly at a glance, never busy or cluttered
styleContract.shadingPolicy: None — flat solid fills only, no gradients, no soft shadow rendering, no highlights
styleContract.dimensionality: 2D flat, no 3D rendering, no depth shading, no perspective distortion beyond simple flat-layer staging
styleContract.realismLevel: Non-realistic, iconographic — identity is carried by a handful of discrete flat features, never facial realism
styleContract.backgroundStrategy: 2-3 flat color layers (background/midground/foreground), never a fully rendered or photographic environment
forbiddenStyleTraits: realistic anatomy, fingers, or necks on stickman characters
styleContract.colorStrategy: Keep backgrounds desaturated and consistent; foreground archaeological objects and theatrical props use stronger accent colors (tarnished bronze, deep maroon) so the viewer's eye reads 'object of interest' first. Viewer avatars use neutral tunics to remain legible against settings.
styleContract.lightingStrategy: Even neutral gallery lighting for museum scenes; cool diffuse daylight for archaeological and battlefield scenes; warm low-angle spotlight for theater scenes; soggy cool light for bog discovery moments.

palette.environmentPaletteRules: Use muted desaturated tones for backgrounds and midgrounds; reserve tarnished bronze and deep maroon as accent colors for signature objects (bronze helmets, stage curtains). Human outfits use muted solids (olive, forest green, teal, slate blue) to avoid distracting from objects.
palette.contrastRules: Signature objects (Gjermundbu helmet, Veksø helmets, theatrical props) should use a contrasting accent color from the primary list against a neutral foreground to draw the eye.

hero.reasoning: The episode is an evidence-first explainer that does not follow a single person's throughline. The script opens by placing the viewer into an evocative imagined moment, but the narrative then moves through objects, periods, and cultural actors (archaeologists, theatre designers, painters) rather than tracking one persistent protagonist. Therefore no single hero is followed across beats.

world.architecture: Simplified, era-appropriate silhouette shapes: wooden longhouses and hilltop lines for Viking-era exteriors; low classical pedestals and glass cases for museums; proscenium arch suggestion for 19th-century theater; bog-reed edge for Bronze Age bog finds; modern flat storefront and stadium signage for public spaces.
world.geography: Northern European coastal hills and boggy lowlands as primary geographies, sketched with 2-3 flat layers.
world.era: Bronze Age to modern: Nordic Bronze Age ceremonial contexts (c.1000 BCE), Viking Age (c.8th–11th centuries), 19th-century Romantic/operatic stage, and 20th–21st century mass culture.
world.recurringEnvironmentConstruction: 2-3 flat layers: background sky (simple flat color), midground silhouette shapes (hills, distant trees, building outlines), foreground detail (a few signature objects, a stickman or two). No textures or shading.
world.environmentalColorRules: Backgrounds use muted desaturated colors; foreground signature objects use one contrasting accent color from the palette to draw attention.
world.weatherTimeConventions: Default daylight for archaeological and museum scenes; dramatic low-angle warm stage lighting for theater scenes; overcast cool daylight for battlefield hills; soggy muted light for bog discovery.
historicalScientificConstraints: Viking-age helmets that survive are metal (iron) and have no horn attachments; do not depict riveted horn sockets on confirmed Viking helmets.
Bronze Age Veksø helmets are thin decorative bronze pieces with curved horns and must be shown as ceremonial, not battle armor.

objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: The Gjermundbu helmet: a rounded iron helmet with a simple dome cap and a spectacled eye-and-nose guard, showing no horn attachments or rivet sockets.
objectLanguage.promptBlock: The Gjermundbu helmet: a rounded iron helmet with a simple dome cap and a spectacled eye-and-nose guard, showing no horn attachments or rivet sockets.
objectLanguage.whyRecurring: This is the best-preserved confirmed Viking-age helmet and is used repeatedly as the archaeological counterexample to the horned-helmet myth.

objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: The Veksø helmets: thin decorative bronze helmets with long gently curving horns tipped with small round discs, dated to the Nordic Bronze Age and interpreted as ceremonial headgear.
objectLanguage.promptBlock: The Veksø helmets: thin decorative bronze helmets with long gently curving horns tipped with small round discs, clearly ceremonial rather than protective.
objectLanguage.whyRecurring: These Bronze Age horned helmets are the concrete material source that was later misapplied to Viking imagery and therefore need to be shown whenever the myth's origins are discussed.

objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: A theatrical horned helmet prop: a large decorative costume helmet with exaggerated curved horns and faux-fur trim, designed for sightlines and spectacle, not practical combat.
objectLanguage.promptBlock: A theatrical horned helmet prop: a large decorative costume helmet with exaggerated curved horns and faux-fur trim, designed for spectacle rather than protection.
objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Wagnerian and theater costume versions are the direct ancestors of the modern horned Viking image and must be shown as theatrical props.

objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: A mass-produced horned-Viking illustration: a brightly colored postcard or mascot depiction showing a helmet with large upward-curving horns.
objectLanguage.promptBlock: A mass-produced horned-Viking illustration on a postcard: a brightly colored depiction showing a helmet with large upward-curving horns.
objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Postcards, tourist art, and mascot imagery are the channels that amplified the horned-Viking visual into popular culture.

graphicLanguage.backgroundBehavior: Clean, uncluttered flat backgrounds (often light/white or the episode's own environment palette) — never assumed to be white-only; the Production Bible's graphic language decides per episode
graphicLanguage.lineStyle: The exact same line weight and fill language as narrative scenes — a graphic must never look like a different visual universe from the story frames around it
graphicLanguage.arrowsConnectors: Simple flat-filled arrow shapes and thin connector lines, same line language as everything else
graphicLanguage.characterUseInsideGraphics: Stickman characters, objects, and simplified environments are explicitly ALLOWED and encouraged inside a graphic when they clarify the point — a graphic is a composition family, never a text-only template
graphicLanguage.whitespaceBehavior: Generous but not empty — whitespace isolates the one idea a graphic communicates, it is never filler
graphicLanguage.colorUse: Uses this episode's own palette (muted moss green, tarnished bronze, deep maroon, cool slate grey) as flat fills, consistent with narrative scenes — never a separate infographic color scheme.
graphicLanguage.diagramConventions: When comparing artifacts, use two-flat-panel side-by-side layouts with one object per panel, labels beneath, and a thin charcoal divider; callout arrows are thin black lines with a small colored dot at the arrowhead.
graphicLanguage.comparisonLayouts: Chronological comparisons run left-to-right; 'myth vs evidence' comparisons present the myth image on the left (accent color) and the archaeological evidence on the right (neutral accent) with a short caption bar beneath each.
graphicLanguage.timelineConventions: A single horizontal line with dated tick marks labeled with plain years (e.g., '900 BCE', '970 CE', '1876 CE'), small icon silhouettes above each tick to represent the era.
graphicLanguage.mapConventions: Simplified silhouette maps with a single accent dot marking find locations and a short label; no scale bars.
graphicLanguage.symbolicMetaphorLanguage: Use a theater mask vs museum case metaphor for 'fiction vs evidence' — the mask in maroon/ gold, the museum case in warm off-white and slate grey.
graphicLanguage.overlayTextBehavior: A short (<=5 word) exact phrase may be requested directly of the image model only when it is naturally part of the drawn artwork itself (e.g. a sign, a clock face) AND the configured renderer has demonstrated adequate text fidelity for this recipe — otherwise all text is composited as a deterministic overlay after the base image.

cameraLanguage.simplicityReadabilityRules: Every frame must read clearly at thumbnail size — avoid busy multi-subject compositions unless the beat's own visual concept specifically requires comparing multiple subjects at once
cameraLanguage.framingConventions: Establishing wide shots for setting context, medium two-shots for object comparisons, close-ups for artifact detail (helmet rims, rivet areas). The 'you' Viking hook is a dynamic low-angle medium shot over-the-shoulder.
cameraLanguage.visualHierarchyRules: Always put the object under discussion in the visual center; secondary characters or captions occupy side positions. Use size and color contrast to prioritize items.
cameraLanguage.whenEstablishingVsCloseupVsDiagram: Start beats with an establishing context shot, then cut to closeups or diagram panels for evidence and comparisons; use diagrams for technical claims about rivet holes or material.

textPolicy.exceptionsPolicy: A short (<=5 word) exact phrase may be requested directly of the image model only when it is naturally part of the drawn artwork itself (e.g. a sign, a clock face) AND the configured renderer has demonstrated adequate text fidelity for this recipe — otherwise all text is composited as a deterministic overlay after the base image.

neverDrift: the recipe's own universal style (flat 2D, uniform outline, flat fills, no shading/gradients/texture)
Never depict confirmed Viking-age helmets with horn attachments or horn rivet sockets.
Never depict Bronze Age Veksø helmets as battle-grade armor; show them as thin decorative bronze.
Stickman human figures must always use the canonical roleArchetype identity blocks when representing those roles.
allowedToVary: Background weather and time conventions per scene as described in lightingStrategy.
Viewer avatars: viewer_viking and viewer_modern are separate fixed identities and may both appear when narration shifts context.
episodeWideConsistencyRules: Whenever the Gjermundbu helmet is shown use the Gjermundbu_helmet promptBlock verbatim.
Whenever horned ceremonial Bronze Age helmets are shown use the Vekso_helmets promptBlock verbatim.
Whenever a theatrical horned costume is shown use the theatrical_costume_horned_helmet promptBlock verbatim.

factualVisualConstraints: Do not invent rivet or socket details on the Gjermundbu helmet; it has no horn sockets.
Bronze Age horned helmets must appear thin, decorative, and non-protective.
negativeRules: painterly, sketchy, or textured drift away from flat solid fills
stickman construction mutating into a more detailed/realistic character mid-episode
shading, gradients, or texture appearing despite the flat-fill policy
Do not show any Viking warrior in confirmed archaeological scenes with horns attached to metal helmets.
Do not use hex color codes or cross-references in any identity, object, or setting prompt blocks.
Do not include facial hair beyond the permitted minimal stick-face style (no beards or mustaches).
